stories.title: Podcast: Reducing CRE Energy Costs with Physical AI, with R-Zero CEO Jennifer Nuckles
stories.excerpt: Jennifer Nuckles is CEO of R-Zero, a physical AI platform that connects building data to continuously uncover energy savings and improve performance, delivering 20-40% HVAC energy savings with no major retrofit required. She previously served as EVP at SoFi and CMO at Zynga, and spent nearly a decade as a Global Business Lead at Clorox. She is a board member and chairperson of the American Lung Association and a trustee at UC Riverside. Based in San Francisco. (02:04) From room intelligence to physical AI (03:51) Buildings have known about waste for decades (05:00) What changed: hardware costs, software, and regulation (07:33) Energy as a constraint (08:12) Local Law 97 (10:08) The end of piloting: choosing and deploying (11:20) R=Zero model (14:23) Building efficiency investments (17:40) Savings Expectations: Qualcomm, Stanford Children’s (21:03) Energy as an NOI lever: 20-40% HVAC savings (23:53) The autonomous building continuum (25:22) What building owners get wrong about energy operations (28:32) Collaboration superpower: Walt Disney and Yannick Noah Learn more: –Visit R-Zero –Jennifer Nuckles on LinkedIn In-person Events: –Finance Forum: NYC | 11/3 –State of Office Forum: NYC | 11/4 –Breakthrough Awards Breakfast: NYC | 12/2 –All upcoming Commercial Observer events Virtual Events: –Spotlight Case Study: Inside the AI Transformation at Cushman & Wakefield: 10/8 –AI & Innovation Forum: 11/18 Connect with Tangent: -Edward Cohen on LinkedIn -Zach Aarons on LinkedIn -Tangent on LinkedIn
bullets: R-Zero delivers 20-40% HVAC energy savings via software, no major retrofit.
Local Law 97 and regulatory pressure driving building efficiency investments.

stories.summary: R-Zero, a physical AI platform, helps building owners cut HVAC energy costs 20–40% through software-driven optimization without major retrofit, addressing regulatory mandates like NYC's Local Law 97. Energy efficiency is increasingly recognized as an NOI lever for owners, though adoption and operational discipline remain barriers. The company operates in San Francisco and is gaining traction with enterprises like Qualcomm and Stanford Children's.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers, energy efficiency and automation are becoming baseline competitive features, especially in regulated metros (NYC, CA). Factoring $0.15–0.25/sf/yr in HVAC savings into pro forma NOI strengthens underwriting and refinance economics, and positions new assets to command rent premiums or faster absorption in sustainability-conscious markets.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges $96M Refi for 1,461-Unit SoCal Portfolio
stories.excerpt: E&S Ring has secured refinancing from Voya Investment Management for a six-property multifamily portfolio in Southern California. Northmarq on Thursday announced the $95.8 million refinancing for the 1,461-unit portfolio. The firm’s Nathan Prouty, Andrew Slaton and John Holt facilitated the deal. The refinance covers existing debt across the portfolio, including four loans from Voya in 2007. The new financing is structured as six non-cross-collateralized loans, and includes a combination of fixed- and floating-rate debt, interest-only payments and prepayment provisions. Four properties are in Los Angeles neighborhoods, one is in Culver City, and the sixth is in Victorville. The portfolio includes the 168-unit Casa Granada and 183-unit Sunset Barrington Gardens in Brentwood; the 117-unit Meadows South in Culver City; the 400-unit Mountain Vista in Victorville; the 317-unit Rancho Los Feliz in Los Feliz; and the 276-unit Villa Vicente in Mid-Wilshire. Greater Los Angeles multifamily vacancy held at 4.5 percent through the first half of the year, while average rent remained slightly below the level from one year ago, according to Northmarq’s most recent numbers. Investment activity accelerated, with more than 40 percent more properties trading in the first half than during the same period in 2025. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: E&S Ring secures $95.8M refi via Voya for 1,461-unit SoCal portfolio.
Six non-cross-collateralized loans; four LA-area properties, Culver City, Victorville.
LA multifamily vacancy 4.5%; refi signals strong portfolio performance.
stories.summary: Northmarq arranged a $95.8 million refinancing for E&S Ring's six-property, 1,461-unit Southern California multifamily portfolio, structured as non-cross-collateralized loans with mixed fixed/floating rates and interest-only provisions. Properties span Los Angeles neighborhoods (Brentwood, Los Feliz, Mid-Wilshire), Culver City, and Victorville. The deal underscores strong occupancy and lender confidence in the LA market, where vacancy sat at 4.5%.
stories.impact: Tight LA vacancy (4.5%) and successful refi activity signal sustained rent growth and portfolio value resilience in coastal CA submarkets. Developers should prioritize acquisitions and groundbreakings in LA proper and adjacent Culver City now, before cap rates compress further and land scarcity limits future starts. Victorville presence hints at inland secondary growth.

stories.title: Grover Corlew Buys Discounted Fort Lauderdale Tower for $70M
stories.excerpt: Development company Grover Corlew has paid $69.7 million for 200 East Broward in Downtown Fort Lauderdale, making it the latest office building to sell for a discount in the South Florida submarket. The 21-story tower features 235,211 square feet of office space adjacent to Southeast Third Avenue, and across the street from a federal courthouse. The 447,253-square-foot property — which is 75 percent occupied — was built in 1991, according to a representative for the Boca Raton-based investor. Grover Corlew, led by principals Mark Corlew and Anuj Grover, plans to spend $20 million over the next two years updating the building to add an amenity deck with a gym and conference facilities. JLL’s Hermen Rodriguez and Ike Ojala brokered the sale, which resulted in a nearly 15 percent loss in value for the seller, Banyan Street Capital, which dropped $81.5 million to acquire the asset in 2017, according to property records. (A representative for the Miami-based Banyan Street did not immediately respond to a comment.) In recent years, a slew of office towers in Fort Lauderdale have sold at a discount. In September, Moishe Mana bought the 30-story 110 Tower for $89 million, about 21 percent less than the $112.9 million the seller had paid a decade ago. Last year, German asset manager DWS sold two office buildings for over $400 million, about the same it had paid. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Grover Corlew buys 21-story office tower, 200 East Broward, $69.7M.
Seller (Banyan Street Capital) took 15% loss; building 75% occupied.
Grover Corlew plans $20M, two-year amenity deck and gym retrofit.
stories.summary: Grover Corlew acquired Downtown Fort Lauderdale's 200 East Broward, a 21-story, 447,253-sf office tower, for $69.7 million—nearly 15% below the seller's 2017 purchase price of $81.5 million. The asset is 75% occupied. Grover Corlew intends to spend $20 million over two years on amenities including a gym and conference facilities to reposition the building.
stories.impact: Office-to-residential conversion or adaptive reuse opportunity: a distressed office tower in a recovering South Florida submarket at a steep discount signals developer appetite for value-add repositioning. Monitor whether Grover Corlew pursues residential conversion (common in South Florida); if so, expect supply gains in Fort Lauderdale multifamily, which could pressure rents or accelerate absorption of existing competitive stock. Office distress in secondary downtowns creates multifamily development windows.

stories.excerpt: Draper and Kramer, Incorporated, announced that James Hayes, chief financial officer for the Chicago-based company, was appointed by Illinois Governor JB Pritzker to serve as a member of the state’s Teachers’ Retirement System Board of Trustees. Once confirmed by the state Senate, Hayes will join the 15-member board in providing fiduciary oversight and strategic direction for one of the largest public pension systems in the United States, with assets and investments totaling more than $85 billion. Syska Hennessy Group, an international engineering firm, has promoted Clint Moreno to principal. He is based in the Chicago office. Moreno has 28 years of experience in the design and management of telecommunications and electrical systems. He specializes in technology infrastructure, including wireless, structured cabling, and network design, for corporate headquarters and critical facilities. His work in critical facilities encompasses several local data centers and projects for a multinational software client. JLL has hired Patrick Miller as the new global president for its technology sector. In his new role, Miller oversees strategic account management and the delivery of customized real estate management solutions that help technology companies worldwide navigate evolving business and workplace needs through data-driven insights. Miller now oversees a team of more than 8,300 experts delivering integrated facilities management and workplace solutions. Cushman & Wakefield announced the addition of Peter Adamo, Adam Lawler and Madeline Leland to its Chicago office leasing and capital markets teams. Adamo and Lawler will serve as Executive Managing Directors, while Leland joins as Transaction Manager. The strategic hires strengthen the firm’s ability to serve investors and owners across Chicago’s suburban office market, adding deep local expertise in lease-up strategy, office capital markets and investment sales for clients’ properties and portfolios. stories.summary: Mast Capital is completing the 80-story Cipriani Residences in Miami's Brickell and is now marketing the 26-story Banyan Tree Residences in West Palm Beach—88 units starting at $1.9M one-bedroom, construction slated for 2027. CIO Jordan Kornberg cited West Palm's walkability, dining, and momentum from office-using job growth and population inflows, positioning it as a next-tier Florida growth market.
stories.impact: West Palm Beach is absorbing luxury residential supply and attracting major developers, signaling a secondary-to-primary market transition. For competitors in South Florida, this implies rising acquisition costs and increased competition for land; for those NOT yet active in West Palm, the window to acquire developable parcels at sub-Miami pricing is narrowing. Monitor office-to-residential conversion potential as WPB office space softens.

stories.title: Carnegie Diner & Cafe Operator to Open New Restaurant at 7 Penn Plaza
stories.excerpt: Carnegie Hospitality is opening its next Carnegie Diner & Cafe in Manhattan’s Penn District. The restaurateur signed on the dotted line last month to take over fast-casual chain Smashburger’s lease at the Feil Organization’s 7 Penn Plaza, Commercial Observer has learned. The tri-party deal included a 10-year lease extension for the 5,609-square-foot retail space at the corner of Seventh Avenue and West 31st Street. Newmark‘s Jeffrey Roseman represented Carnegie in the deal, while the Feil Organization’s Randall Briskin negotiated in-house for the landlord. The asking rent was not disclosed, but retail rents in the nearby Herald Square shopping corridor averaged $412 per square foot in the first half of 2026, according to the Real Estate Board of New York. Carnegie Diner plans to open in the Penn District in November, a Newmark spokesperson told CO. Its space spans a 3,110-square-foot ground floor, an 865-square-foot mezzanine level and a 1,634-square-foot basement. Carnegie’s new neighbors at 7 Penn — which also has an address of 370 Seventh Avenue — include bagel chain PopUp Bagels, açaí shop Oakberry Açaí, and popular lunch spots Sweetgreen and Naya. Cap Street Advisors‘ Gui Tepedino represented Smashburger in its share of the deal. The burger chain’s website currently lists one remaining location in Manhattan at 804 Lexington Avenue. It operates several more in the city’s outer boroughs. “Smashburger has made the decision to transition out of our 7th and Penn restaurant in New York City as we focus on our broader New York metro locations,” a spokesperson for the chain told CO in a statement. Carnegie Hospitality currently operates nine New York City locations, the majority of which operate as Carnegie Diner & Cafe. Carnegie also runs two stand-alone restaurant concepts: Delos Greek Restaurant at 102 West 47th Street and Voco Roofbar at 170 West 48th Street. stories.title: Automation is Reshaping, Not Erasing, Manufacturing Jobs
stories.excerpt: Automation isn’t wiping out U.S. manufacturing jobs. Rather, it’s restructuring them, according to a recent CBRE report. Multiple manual jobs are being replaced with fewer, more technical ones. But, “the work is changing faster than the workforce being trained for it, presenting a considerable challenge for manufacturers and the communities that depend on them,” CBRE said. CBRE explained that the jobs exposed to automation tend to be repetitive, predictable and physically demanding. Pick-and-place assembly, spot welding, basic quality inspection and moving materials between workstations can be handled by robots, which offer greater speed and precision and lower cost per unit for many of these tasks. Among the occupations CBRE tracked, employment fell the most for hand packers and packagers, and for machinists, from 2016 to 2025, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Machinist employment dropped more than 25%. Over the same period, employment of industrial engineers rose nearly 43%, and employment of industrial machinery mechanics increased by 31%. Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians grew by 13%. “Economists call this shift job polarization: automation absorbs repetitive, rule-based tasks and raises the value of judgment, adaptability and complex decision-making,” the report said. CBRE added that today’s manufacturing facilities require a different workforce than the ones they’re replacing, with the following categories: Automation technicians and robotics maintenance specialists diagnose and repair robots, robot cells and conveyor systems. The jobs rarely require an engineering degree but pay well above production work. Process engineers and automation systems integrators design workflows that combine human and robotic labor. As more manufacturers adopt AI, these jobs include machine vision, predictive maintenance, digital twins and AI-enabled process optimization. bullets: Manufacturing automation reduces manual jobs; 25% machinist decline 2016–2025.
Industrial engineers +43%, industrial machinery mechanics +31%, technicians +13%.
Job polarization: repetitive tasks absorbed, technical roles valued higher.
stories.summary: A CBRE report finds automation is restructuring, not eliminating, U.S. manufacturing jobs. Manual roles (hand packers, machinists) fell sharply (machinists down 25% from 2016–2025), while technical roles (industrial engineers +43%, machinery mechanics +31%, technicians +13%) expanded. The mismatch between job losses and new skills required poses challenges for manufacturers and dependent communities.
stories.impact: Manufacturing restructuring reduces demand for unskilled labor in industrial-dependent regions (Midwest, Southeast), dampening multifamily renter pool growth in secondary metros tied to legacy manufacturing. However, rising technical job creation (engineers, technicians) creates pockets of professional-class demand. Developers should avoid speculative multifamily overbuilding in single-industry manufacturing towns; favor mixed-income product in diversified metros with growing technical/professional employment.

stories.title: Shrinking Construction Pipelines Could Extend CRE Rent-Growth Runway
stories.excerpt: When determining commercial real estate strategies, many investors focus on demand. However, Marcus & Millichap’s October 2026 Construction Outlook research brief said that demand tells only half the story. Long-term supply trends also affect vacancy and rent growth, so supply outlooks should play a prominent role in CRE planning. Construction tends to lag market conditions, leading to movement between too much and not enough capacity. When supply tightens, vacancies drop, and rents increase, prompting more development. Too much development can lead to increased vacancies and pressure on rents. Marcus & Millichap said that not all asset types move in sync; each has its own cycle. Additionally, macro factors and structural shifts can impact the pattern of those cycles. Additionally, three forces have been impacting current development activity: Higher interest rates have pushed up financing costs and made fewer projects feasible. Tariffs and elevated shipping costs are keeping building material prices high. Labor costs are under pressure from immigration policy and from strong demand tied to AI and data center development. With costs elevated, the firm expects new projects to stay limited until rents rise enough to support construction economics. That slowdown could make the falling vacancy and rising rent phase of the cycle last longer than it has historically. The pullback is already evident in the pipelines: Apartments: units under construction are down 50% from their 2023 peak and still falling. Industrial: space under construction has dropped 60% from its 2022 peak, and continues to contract. Self-storage: construction investment is down 32% from its 2023 peak. Seniors housing and medical office: both are seeing similar declines. Retail and office: construction remains limited, and higher building costs will likely push back the next development cycle in both sectors. bullets: Construction pipelines shrinking due to elevated costs, financing tightness.
Marcus & Millichap: supply shortfalls extend falling-vacancy, rising-rent phase.
Next building cycle may delay several years; rents stay elevated.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap's October 2026 Construction Outlook warns that shrinking pipelines—driven by high costs, tight lending, and weak developer economics—are extending the supply-constrained phase of the CRE cycle. Falling vacancy and rising rents will persist longer than historical norms because new starts remain suppressed until rents rise enough to support construction. The next oversupply cycle could be delayed several years.
stories.impact: FOR MULTIFAMILY DEVELOPERS: This is the critical signal. Restricted new supply by competitors (especially in high-cost coastal metros) means: (1) strong rent growth runway for stabilized portfolios through late 2027–2028; (2) elevated cap rates on value-add/development sites, justifying aggressive land acquisition now before competition returns; (3) urgency to lock in financing and entitlements while construction costs remain fixed. Delay = risk of being priced out as other developers re-enter markets. Pursue starts aggressively in 2026–2027.

stories.title: Holiday Budgets Climb 9.7% as Shoppers Trim Gift Lists
stories.excerpt: U.S. shoppers plan to spend $1,243 on the holidays this season, up 9.7% from last year, according to JLL’s recently released 2026 holiday shopping survey. However, the extra money is going to the celebration rather than the presents, as gift spending budgets barely moved. “After a season of trimming in 2025, Americans are determined to have a happy holiday season this year, replete with delicious food, festive décor and fun holiday experiences,” the report said. Furthermore: Gift budgets increased by 3.1% year-over-year, making up 48.1% of the season’s budget Spending on food and decorations is up by 16% Funds directed to entertainment and dining out increased by 17.3% “In 2025, the advice to centers was simple. Keep shoppers longer, and they will spend more,” the report said. But this year, the advice changed a bit. Longer isn’t better. Planned spending peaks at $1,594 for shoppers expecting to stay 60 to 75 minutes, then drops to $1,217 for those staying longer than 90 minutes. This year, the increase is in the number of stores a shopper plans to visit. Shoppers planning one or two retail categories budget about $570, while those planning seven or more budget just over $2,000. “Stretching a visit takes benches, music and coffee. Widening one takes cross-category offers, clear directories and signage that points people toward stores they had not planned on, and it reaps bigger rewards,” JLL said. JLL said that the share of shoppers planning a mall visit rose to 55.3% from 49.9 percent in 2025. And, while online delivery still led the way, it fell to 80% from 83.9% the year before. JLL also pointed out that: 20.8% of shoppers said they plan to buy something to eat or drink on each trip, up from 12.2% in 2025 Planned shopping on Black Friday fell to 39,8% in-store and 55.1% online Cyber Monday shopping dropped to 46.9% from 55.2% In-store shopping on Thanksgiving day rose to 31.8% from 25.8%, driven by households earning over $150,000. bullets: Holiday spending budgets up 9.7% YoY to $1,243 per shopper.
Gift spending flat; extra $ allocated to food, décor, experiences.
Peak spending $1,594 for 60–75 min visits; 90+ min drops to $1,217.
stories.summary: JLL's 2026 holiday shopping survey shows U.S. shoppers plan $1,243 spending, up 9.7% YoY, but increased discretionary spend goes to celebration (food, décor, experiences) rather than gifts. Shoppers spending most ($1,594) stay 60–75 minutes; longer visits (90+ min) yield lower spend ($1,217). Retail centers should focus on cross-category store exposure and wayfinding to drive multi-store trips rather than dwell time.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily relevance. Retail spending patterns and center traffic do not materially shape apartment demand, supply, or capital flows. Consumer confidence signals are tangential and already priced into broader economic forecasts.

stories.title: Senior Housing Occupancy Hits 90.4% as Supply Gap Widens
stories.excerpt: Senior housing has moved from a healthcare real estate niche to a sector that warrants close watch, according to a recent Northmarq guide for potential investors. Understanding the Numbers The National Investment Center for Seniors Housing & Care (NIC) said that occupancy across 31 primary markets in Q3 2026 reached 90.4%, marking the 21st consecutive quarter of gains. Independent living and assisted living occupancies averaged 91.7% and 89.1%, respectively. At the same time, rising construction costs, higher interest rates, and tighter construction lending are slowing groundbreakings. Most new projects are in Sun Belt growth corridors and in the suburbs of major metros. NIC reported that just over 16,000 units were under construction in the primary markets in the second quarter, split between independent and assisted living. Inventory growth held steady at 0.4% annually. “Holding national occupancy at 90% as the population ages would require more than 100,000 new units in most years through the late 2030s,” NIC said. “The current pace of development is 10,445 per year—roughly 10% of that requirement.” Different from Multifamily One issue unique to senior housing is what it includes. Northmarq breaks the sector into five categories: independent living, assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing and low-income senior housing. Independent living operates most like a conventional multifamily. Skilled nursing is the most operationally intensive and the most tied to government reimbursement. “For investors coming from conventional multifamily real estate, the biggest adjustment is understanding that senior housing is an operating business layered on top of real estate,” the report said. “Property performance is tied directly to the quality and stability of the operator, not just the physical asset or the local rental market.” In addition to operator expertise and quality, other factors that impact senior housing value include: Proximity to adult children and medic
bullets: Senior housing occupancy 90.4% across 31 primary markets, Q3 2026.
21 consecutive quarters of gains; 16K units under construction, 0.4% annual growth.
NIC: 100K+ units/yr needed through late 2030s; current pace 10.4K/yr.
stories.summary: National Investment Center for Seniors Housing & Care (NIC) reports Q3 2026 occupancy reached 90.4% across 31 primary markets—the 21st consecutive quarter of improvement. Just over 16,000 units were under construction (split independent/assisted living); annual inventory growth held at 0.4%. NIC estimates 100,000+ new units annually are needed through the late 2030s to maintain 90% occupancy as the population ages, but current development pace delivers only 10,445 units/year—roughly 10% of the requirement.
stories.impact: MASSIVE MULTIFAMILY PROXY SIGNAL: Senior housing supply undershooting demand by 90% creates structural tailwind for age-restricted and mixed-age multifamily in Sun Belt growth corridors (TX, FL, AZ, GA) where NIC reports new projects concentrate. Developers should consider senior-friendly features (single-level accessibility, services) in 55+ communities and urban mixed-use projects targeting empty-nesters. Rising senior occupancy and cost inflation (construction, lending) mean aggressive institutional operators will consolidate supply; independent developers face margin pressure. Scout land in Tampa, Phoenix, Charlotte submarkets NOW.
